newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe rail workers join wave of pay strikes.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe rail workers join wave of pay strikes.

text.p: Thousands of Zimbabwean railway workers joined a wave of wildcat strikes sweeping the southern African state on Wednesday, ignoring calls by President Robert Mugabe to negotiate their demands for higher pay.
Union officials said more than 11,000 employees of the National Railways of Zimbabwe (NRZ) had walked out to press demands for a 58 percent wage increase.
The strike has hit passenger and goods train movements around the country, but NRZ officials said they hoped to restore services soon after talks with the strikers.

"They went off in anger while we were still negotiating their proposals," a senior railway manager said by telephone interview from Bulawayo in southwestern Zimbabwe where the NRZ has its headquarters.
"We were taken by surprise," he said, refusing to be identified.

But Zvavamwe Shambare, the secretary-general of the Railway Artisans' Union (RAU), and Lovemore Shana, leader of the main Zimbabwe Amalgamated Railwaymen's Union (ZARU), both accused management of intransigence in the pay talks, saying strike action was the only language they understood.
President Mugabe appealed to Zimbabwean workers earlier on Wednesday to desist from strikes before exhausting negotiation channels.

"Workers should not succumb to the sense of indiscipline. Arguments should be presented well and not rush into strikes because they have an adverse effect if they become the only resort to failed negotiations," he told Zimbabwe state media.

Employees in some construction companies, clothing and textile industries went on strike on Tuesday demanding salary rises of over 40 percent, saying the economy -- expected to grow by about six percent this year after a seven-percent rise in 1996 -- can afford it.
Other industries that have suffered wildcat strikes in the last few weeks include banking, transport, hotel and catering where workers have demanded annual pay increases of between 25 and 60 percent.

The Employers Confederation of Zimbabwe and the Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions have for weeks been trying to find a way of curtailing the strikes, which they say is affecting productivity and has devastating effects on the general economy.
Some bank employees threatened to go back on strike on Thursday if their pay demands were not met.
